GIUSEPPE ROCCA (b Barbaresco, Alba, 1807; d San Francesco d'Albaro, Genoa, 1865) A VIOLIN AFTER STRADIVARI (d716), Turin, 1852, The handsome one-piece back of medium to broad curl ascending from left to right, the ribs of medium curl, the head of similar curl and bearing substantial traces of the original black paintwork to the edges, the table of medium grain, the varnish, in a largely untouched state, of a rich red-brown colour over a golden ground, Labelled Joseph Rocca fecit Taurini anno Domini 1852 IHS and inscribed G.R. in the mortice of the pegbox, Length of back 14in. (35.6cm.), This instrument retains the original neck undisturbed and probably the original fingerboard. See The Strad (August 1992, p. 719) for a comparison of scrolls cut by Giuseppe Rocca with dates given as 1848 and 1864, Writing in 1891, Hill notes in the monograph on The Salabue Stradivari (pp. 25 & 26) that 'There can be no doubt that the Salabue violin has exercised a strong influence on modern copyists. The Turin maker, Pressenda (1777 to 1854), who was acquainted with Count Salabue, and his pupil Rocca (d.1862) (sic), who knew Tarisio, were evidently familiar with the instrument. Rocca in particular would seem to have made it his ideal, for we find reproduced in nearly all his copies of Stradivari the characteristic sharp bordering ridge, slanting soundholes, and general flat model of the Salabue.' In the postscript, which appears in later editions of the same treatise on the 'Messiah', Hills illustrate an example by Rocca, undated, with related text on p. 34: 'Also ... a few photographs of some interesting copies, the first one being by J.B. Rocca (sic) which shows that he had access to the violin before it left Italy...' Goodkind (Violin Iconography of Antonio Stradivari, p. 476) supports this point by illustrating, next to the pictorial entry of the 'Messiah' itself, a different example by Rocca, to that of the Hill postscript, captioned '1716 Messiah (copy by Jos. Rocca - 1851)', and gives some of the provenance of it in the appendices. Another model for Giuseppe Rocca's reproductions was a Violin by Giuseppe Guarneri del Gesù, dated 1742, which in subsequent years was presented by Jean Baptiste Vuillaume to his son-in-law, Delphin Alard (see Groves, Dictionary of Musical Instruments, Vol. 3 p. 253)
